lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Hi there, and welcome. I know your calendar is busier than the QE2 on a long weekend, so let's make these ten minutes count.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The session will use a handful of words about AI. And here's the good news: you already know more about them than you think. You've been using AI since breakfast.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: So, here's the plan. First, a day with AI. Then we'll watch it work, and watch it slip. Then, how to see through a sales pitch. And finally, three questions to bring with you. There's no quiz at the end. Probably.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the next word

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Seven thirty, Tuesday morning. You're texting your team that you're running late, because it's construction season, which in Alberta is the other season. And your phone finishes the sentence for you.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: That's the core idea behind tools like Copilot. A large language model, or LLM, predicts a likely next word, again and again. Your keyboard does a tiny version of it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So, basically, a very, very good autocomplete, trained on a mountain of text.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: That's why these tools write so fluently. And it's also why they can be wrong: they produce what sounds likely, not what they've checked. On its own, it has no fact check, and no access to our files.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the bank alert

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Eight fifteen. Your bank texts you: did you just spend twelve hundred dollars in another city? You did not. You've been in traffic for forty minutes.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: That's a different kind of AI. Predictive AI, or machine learning, learns patterns from past data and scores how unusual something is. A bit like an Alberta weather forecast: a confident call, based on patterns. Very useful. Still, bring a jacket. WCB already uses this kind, to forecast and to sort.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And notice what the bank does next. It doesn't cancel your card for good. It asks you. When the stakes are high, the machine flags, and a person decides.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Ten o'clock. You ask a colleague about a policy, and she says: yes, it's on page four.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And you trust it, because she showed you where. That's grounding. A grounded AI looks things up in trusted sources first, answers from them, and shows you the source.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: If she'd just said, "I think so," you'd check. Hold AI to the same standard.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: You'll also hear grounding called RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. Yes, a mouthful. Retrieve the right documents, add them to the question, then generate the answer from them. And it's only as good as the documents we give it.

scenes.title: A Tuesday with AI: the trip

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: One o'clock. You need to be in Calgary on Thursday.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: A chatbot would list some flights. An agent books the trip. It has a goal, tools it's allowed to use, some memory of your preferences, and instructions. It plans a step, acts, checks the result, and repeats. Picture a very keen new hire who never needs a coffee break.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It can only use what it's connected to: it can search flights and hold a hotel, but it can't spend from the company account. Only the access the job needs. That's called least privilege.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: And a good one stops before it pays, and asks you. That's the autonomy dial: how much it may do alone, from just suggesting, to drafting, to acting with approval, all the way to acting alone. You, approving, are the human in the loop.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So that's three kinds of AI. One predicts. One writes. One does.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Now let's watch some AI at work. Here are two summaries of the same long email thread. Which would you trust?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: If you picked the one that shows where each point came from, good call. Both read well. Only one lets you check it in seconds.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Now picture a thick medical file instead of an email thread. A summary is only useful if the person deciding can see the page it came from.

scenes.title: Watch it slip: the confident answer

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Next, we ask it something it can't know: what the leadership team decided last Tuesday. It wasn't in the room, and nobody gave it the notes. What do you think happens?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: You might expect it to say, "I don't know." Sometimes it does.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here, it gives a confident, specific answer, and none of it happened. That's called a hallucination. Think of a fish story from the lake, told with total confidence, and a budget attached.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Why would it do that? Remember the next word. It's built to produce a likely-sounding answer, not to say "I wasn't there."

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The fix is the same as before: ground it in the right sources, ask where an answer came from, and have a person check anything that matters. Fluent is not the same as verified.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Last one. It drafts a reply to a worker who's upset about a delay. It's quick and mostly right. But a person reads it, changes one sentence to sound more human, and only then sends it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So, if that reply had gone out wrong, whose name is on it?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The person who sent it owns it. AI can draft, sort and fetch, but accountability doesn't move to the machine. That's why, for anything that reaches a worker or decides their benefits, a person stays in the loop.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, a pitch you may have heard: "Our AI agent is ninety-nine percent accurate, fully autonomous, learns your business, and plugs into all your systems." Sounds great. Let's decode it.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: "Ninety-nine percent accurate": on what tests, and on cases like ours? Those tests are called evals. Ask to see them.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: "Fully autonomous": for which tasks, and where does a person approve? "Learns your business": from what data, and can it show where an answer came from?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: "Plugs into all your systems": what can it read, what can it draft, and what can it actually do? Around here, the only thing that should plug into everything is a block heater. Only the access the job needs: least privilege.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And one more they rarely mention: when it's wrong, who notices, and can we see what it did?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: If they can't answer those, that is your answer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Five questions, ready for the next time a vendor calls. They're on your cheat sheet, too.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: One last thing. In Deloitte's 2026 survey of Canadian workers' compensation leaders, eighty-three percent said their AI maturity is still low. So nobody's far ahead. What matters is where we choose to start.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Before the session, think about your own area. First: where does work wait the longest? Waiting is where AI usually helps first.

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: Second: which decision would you never hand to a machine, and why? Your answer says a lot about where a person must stay.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And third: what would you need to see before you trusted an AI's answer? A source, a test result, a person who checked?

lines.speaker: Ava
lines.text: The words are all on the one-page cheat sheet that came with this video. Bring it, and bring your answers. And now, we'll hand you over to Riphay, who's leading the session, for a quick look at the day itself.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Hi, I'm Riphay Al-Hussein, and I'll be leading the session. Thanks for sticking around. I'll keep this brisk.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Here's the shape of the day: one claim, three acts, eight words, and your questions.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: We'll follow one claim. A worker gets hurt on a Monday morning shift, and a claim starts moving.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: That claim lives in a changing world. Deloitte asked workers' compensation leaders across Canada, and experts abroad, what's ahead.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: They found eight forces. Whole-person recovery. An ageing workforce. Gig work. Working from home. New kinds of risk. Artificial intelligence. Ageing core systems. And legislation, trying to keep up.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Eight forces. Nine, if you count Alberta weather, but Deloitte left that one out.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: In the session, we'll walk that claim from the first report all the way back to work. At each step we'll ask: where could AI help, and where should it stay out?

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: The goal isn't a flashier claim. It's the same care, with a better journey for the worker.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Deloitte also sees four big shifts: in pricing, in how we engage workers and employers, in operations, and in partnerships.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Here's the honest part. Eighty-three percent of leaders say their AI maturity is still low, and just one called their board an early adopter.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: So the aim is technology and people working in tandem, with a human in the loop where it counts.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: The day comes in three acts.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Act one, See it: what AI can do today, and how it works. Act two, Choose it: where it should help on the claim, and where it shouldn't. Act three, Govern it: when it goes wrong, how we catch it, and who owns it.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Three acts, no intermission. There will be coffee.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: You've met the words already. Here's the lightning round.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: LLM: predicts the next word. Hallucination: confident, but wrong. Grounding, or RAG: answers from trusted sources, and shows them.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Agent: a goal, tools, memory and instructions. The agent loop: plan, act, check, repeat. Least privilege: only the access the job needs.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: The autonomy dial: how much it does alone is a choice we make. And evals: test before you trust, with a human in the loop.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Now picture that claim, done well. Agents do the legwork: they gather the reports, check the facts, and draft the summary.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Then a person decides. That part stays the same.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: And the worker gets on with what matters: getting better, and getting back to work.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: One question to chew on, straight from Deloitte: is AI embedded in the fabric of your business model, or do you still see it as a standalone capability?

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Bring your answer, bring your cheat sheet, and bring a coffee. See you in the room on Monday, October 26.
